newsitem.title: UK: Enterprise Oil top UK share in class of '96.
newsitem.headline: Enterprise Oil top UK share in class of '96.

text.p: Fuelled by higher crude prices, favourable exploration news and a string of takeovers, the oil production sector pumped up Britain's best-performing stocks in 1996, with Enterprise Oil leading the blue chips.
While the FTSE 100 index of leading shares rose 11.6 percent over the 12 months, repeatedly hitting record highs, Enterprise powered 63.4 percent ahead.
The top performer among the FTSE 250 index of medium sized firms was Cairn Energy Plc, which rose 268 percent on the back of promising drilling operations offshore Bangladesh.

Conglomerates were the year's party poopers with Hanson having the dubious honour of being the year's worst performer in the FTSE 100. The company, which spun off two units in October, fell 30.3 percent.
The price drop has been adjusted for the demerger of the chemicals and tobacco arms, which has left Hanson with its energy and construction operations.

The group's energy business is next in line to be floated off as investors turn their backs on diversified groups, built up in the booming 1980s by business tycoons like Lord Hanson and Tiny Rowland, who built Lonrho Plc.
Shares in Lonrho, a FTSE 250 company comprising hundreds of units, slumped 28.7 percent even though it too started a demerger process after Rowland was ousted in 1995.

Other notable weak spots were B.A.T Industries, the insurance and tobacco firm, down 14.6 percent and the second worst performing FTSE 100 stock, and BTR, the diversified Anglo-Australian manufacturer, which dropped 13.5 percent.

Rather than conglomerates, where shareholders' value can be hard to find, investors sought out companies moving to sharpen their focus, like British Aerospace Plc, which was the FTSE 100's second best performer, and hotels and betting group Ladbroke Group Plc, which came in third.

British Aerospace climbed 60.8 percent as it is regarded as Europe's leading defence company, while it also benefited from a pick-up in the civil aviation market which helped Airbus consortium aircraft sales.

Ladbroke, which hit a four-year high just one week ago, gained an overall 57.7 percent in 1996, helped by an upturn in the British economy and several management decisions such as general cost-cutting measures and a well-timed hotel alliance with Hilton Hotels Corp.
The Hilton sales and marketing deal was struck in August as the hotel business flourished with occupancy rates rising in both Britain and the U.S.

Both Merrill Lynch and NatWest Securities tipped Ladbroke and British Aerospace as outperformers for the new year. Also featuring prominently on their lists were insurance firms and banks such as Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Group Plc, Barclays Plc and Standard Chartered Plc.

Analysts are banking on further consolidation in the financial sector, which is also expected to be lifted by more cost-cutting measures in a benign macro-economic climate characterised by low inflation.
The oil production sector too is seen doing well again in 1997 as continued takeover activity outweighs the negative impact from an expected retreat in crude oil prices during the course of 1997.
"That (the takeover frenzy) will likely outweigh the negatives," said analyst John Toalster at SocGen. "It's hard to be negative."
Five best performing FTSE 100 stocks in 1996
1. Enterprise Oil +63.4 percent
2. British Aerospace +60.8
3. Ladbroke +57.7
4. Hays Plc +49.5
5. Mercury Asset Management Group +42.9
Five worst performing FTSE 100 stocks
1. Hanson -30.3 percent
2. B.A.T Industries -14.6
4. Allied Domecq -13.0
5. Great Universal Stores -10.6
